title: Archon Request Lifecycle
purpose: Follow one request from the browser through governance, execution, evidence, and evaluation.
limitations: This is derivative learning material, not canonical implementation evidence.

study_guide.heading: Learning outcomes
study_guide.body: Explain the full request path, identify deterministic trust boundaries, distinguish execution evidence from evaluation, and describe failure behavior without overclaiming.

study_guide.heading: Mental model
study_guide.body: Think of Archon as a bounded interpreter around a probabilistic model. The model proposes the next step; typed state, schemas, policy, approvals, budgets, and executors constrain what can happen.

study_guide.heading: Entry and identity
study_guide.body: The browser sends a request through the gateway. Authentication establishes caller identity before owner-scoped conversation data or protected tools are exposed.

study_guide.heading: Context and model decision
study_guide.body: The runtime assembles bounded context from conversation state, instructions, skills, and retrieval. The model returns either answer text or structured tool intent.

study_guide.heading: Governed tools
study_guide.body: Schema validation checks shape. Policy returns ALLOW, ASK, or DENY. ASK requires approval bound to the exact effect; only then may the executor run the tool.

study_guide.heading: Evidence and evaluation
study_guide.body: The Run Ledger preserves events and outcomes. Observability explains what happened. Evaluation separately judges groundedness and related qualities.

study_guide.heading: Failure semantics
study_guide.body: Provider errors, budget exhaustion, denied tools, and timeouts are explicit stop conditions. A timeout is not a pass, and a mock is not live evidence.

study_guide.heading: Interview explanation
study_guide.body: Archon separates probabilistic planning from deterministic control. The model can propose a tool call, but schemas, policy, durable approval, bounded execution, and an append-only evidence trail determine whether and how it runs.

study_guide.heading: What this does not prove
study_guide.body: This guide does not prove public deployment, universal provider behavior, benchmark performance, or capabilities marked deferred in canonical evidence.

audio_script.text: Imagine an AI agent not as an autonomous employee with unlimited authority, but as a probabilistic planner inside a deterministic control system. That is the central mental model for Archon. A user request begins in the browser, but it does not travel directly to a model and then straight into a tool. It crosses explicit trust boundaries. The gateway routes the request. Authentication establishes the caller. The runtime assembles context and enforces budgets. The model may answer or propose a structured action. Validation, policy, and approval decide whether that proposal can become an effect. Finally, the Run Ledger records what actually happened. This distinction matters because model intent is not execution evidence.

After identity and ownership checks, Archon constructs the model context from bounded conversation history, project instructions, relevant skills, and retrieval results when needed. The runtime behaves like a bounded interpreter. It limits iterations, tool calls, tokens, time, and cost. When the model proposes a tool call, the registry first checks the tool name and argument schema. A valid shape is still not authorization. The policy layer returns one of three outcomes: allow, ask, or deny. Allow can continue immediately. Ask pauses for a durable approval bound to the user, tool, normalized arguments, and execution identity. Deny produces an explicit controlled result. The model cannot approve its own request, and a previous approval cannot silently authorize changed arguments.

Approved execution crosses another boundary. Code execution uses an isolated runner with bounded resources. Other tools return structured results to the runtime. Events, outcomes, usage, and stop reasons are preserved in the Run Ledger so the system can explain what happened. Evaluation is separate: it judges qualities such as groundedness after or around execution, while observability records operational facts. Failures remain part of the contract. A timeout means the deadline was reached; it is not a pass. A mock test proves deterministic wiring, not live provider behavior. A healthy process proves liveness, not complete readiness. And a locally verified stack does not imply public deployment. If you can explain those boundaries clearly, you understand the core of Archon's request lifecycle.

Context is not magical memory. A production agent has several sources of information, and each has a different purpose. Recent conversation messages preserve the immediate exchange. Project instructions constrain behavior for the current workspace. Skills provide reusable procedures selected for the request. Retrieval can add relevant document chunks. Durable memory can preserve approved facts across sessions. The runtime must decide what enters the finite model window, in what order, and under what token budget. Too little context creates blind decisions. Too much context can hide the important evidence or exceed the provider limit. Archon therefore treats context construction as an explicit, observable stage. It can record token estimates and compaction behavior without pretending that a larger prompt is automatically a better prompt. When explaining this in an interview, separate storage from retrieval, retrieval from selection, and selected context from the model's final interpretation.

A tool is not merely a function name. It has a contract: a name, description, argument schema, result shape, permissions, and operational limits. The model sees the callable contract and may propose arguments, but deterministic validation checks that proposal before any handler runs. This protects the runtime from missing fields, unexpected values, and unsupported tool names. After validation, policy evaluates the requested effect. Reads, writes, external calls, and code execution do not carry the same risk. An allow decision means the configured policy permits immediate execution. Ask means a human decision is required. Deny means execution must not occur. This separation is essential because a model can produce syntactically perfect output that is still unauthorized or unsafe. Structured output reduces ambiguity; it does not replace governance.

Human approval must describe the exact action being authorized. Archon binds a durable approval to the owner, run, tool call, tool name, normalized arguments, and an effect identity. If the arguments change, the previous approval is not silently reused. Effect identity also supports idempotency. Distributed systems retry when networks fail or acknowledgements are lost, but repeating a side effect can charge a card twice, send duplicate messages, or modify the same resource more than once. The system therefore records whether an effect was reserved, executed, or completed. Exactly-once behavior cannot be promised universally across every external system, but Archon can enforce an at-most-once boundary for the effects under its durable control. The honest claim is as important as the mechanism.

Once an action is authorized, execution still needs containment. The sandbox runner is a separate service with no network access, a read-only filesystem outside temporary work areas, dropped capabilities, process and memory limits, and a constrained security profile. Those controls reduce blast radius, but they do not make arbitrary code trustworthy. Every tool also has deadlines and bounded output. If execution times out, returns malformed data, or violates a boundary, the runtime records an explicit failure instead of inventing success. The model may receive a sanitized error and decide whether a safe retry is appropriate, but retries remain inside the same budgets and effect rules. This is the practical meaning of resilience: not pretending failures disappear, but containing them and preserving enough evidence to understand the outcome.

The Run Ledger is the durable account of a run. It records ordered events such as model decisions, tool calls, approval states, results, usage, and terminal stop reasons. Observability uses those facts to answer operational questions: what happened, how long it took, where it failed, and which resources were used. Evaluation asks a different question: was the result good? Groundedness, citation quality, or task success are judgments applied to recorded behavior. Keeping these layers separate prevents a common mistake. A beautiful trace does not prove a correct answer, and a high evaluation score does not prove that every operational control worked. Together, the ledger and evaluators create evidence that can be inspected, compared, and discussed without rewriting the original run.

A credible Archon explanation always names the evidence level. Source code proves that an implementation exists. Deterministic tests prove selected contracts under controlled inputs. A local runtime check proves that a retained stack served the behavior on a specific machine. A live-provider run proves that one configured provider completed a real interaction. Public deployment requires separate operational evidence. These levels must not be collapsed. The same discipline applies to learning media. A generated deck or podcast can explain architecture, but it cannot upgrade a capability from deferred to implemented. The strongest interview answer is not a long feature list. It is a precise explanation of where probabilistic reasoning ends, where deterministic controls begin, what was actually observed, and which limitations remain.
